# The Abyss of Time

*"We find no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end."*
— James Hutton, 1788

In June of 1788, a small boat bobbed off the Berwickshire coast of Scotland carrying three men and a radical idea. James Hutton, a farmer and natural philosopher, had brought his friend John Playfair and Sir James Hall to see a cliff face called Siccar Point, and what they saw there rearranged the world. Below them lay two rocks telling two incompatible stories: grey schist standing on end, its layers turned vertical like books shoved sideways on a shelf, and above it, resting flat across the truncated edges, red sandstone laid down in gentle sheets. Between the two stories stretched an absence — the eroded remains of mountains that had risen, been worn down to their roots, and drowned, all before the red stone was deposited. Playfair later confessed that standing there, "the mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far into the abyss of time."

What Hutton understood, and what the cliff made visible, was that the earth keeps two kinds of records: the rock itself, and the gaps between the rocks. The gaps are often the louder testimony. An unconformity is a sentence with the middle torn out, and the missing middle was, in this case, longer than all of recorded history by many thousands of repetitions. Hutton drew the obvious, vertiginous conclusion: the planet's story had no readable first page and no foreseeable last one. No vestige of a beginning. No prospect of an end.

Before Hutton, educated Europeans generally accepted Archbishop Ussher's careful calculation that creation occurred in 4004 BCE, giving the earth a comfortable biography of about six thousand years — long enough for patriarchs and pharaohs, short enough to hold in one narrative breath. After Hutton, the earth acquired a quantity the mind cannot picture, only manipulate. The writer John McPhee eventually gave this quantity a name — *deep time* — and the name stuck because the thing itself refuses to.

Every attempt to feel deep time ends in failure, but the failures are instructive. Compress the earth's 4.54 billion years into a single calendar year and life of any kind appears sometime in March; complex animals don't show up until November; dinosaurs flourish for a week and a half in December; and *Homo sapiens* arrives in the final hours of New Year's Eve. All of recorded history — every empire, scripture, symphony, and war — fits into roughly the last thirty-five seconds. The oldest solid material ever found on earth, zircon crystals from the Jack Hills of Australia, crystallized 4.4 billion years ago, which means we possess grains of sand older than every ocean basin now in existence. We live among relics. We simply rarely notice them.

⁂

Humans noticed deep time late, but we acted against it early. Monument-building may be the oldest expression of the intuition that we are temporary and that this is intolerable. Consider the arithmetic that makes Egyptology strange: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Apollo moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. When she toured the necropolis at Giza, she was visiting antiquities already twenty-five centuries old, gazing at them across a gulf as wide as the one separating her from Neil Armstrong. The pyramid builders aimed at eternity knowing perfectly well they would not see it. That is the strange contract of all monumental architecture: hands that will become dust laying stones meant to outlast dust.

The Gothic cathedrals made the contract explicit. Their architects worked on schedules no human career could satisfy; a master mason might spend forty years on a nave whose towers his grandchildren would not live to see topped. Cologne Cathedral was begun in 1248 and stood unfinished for six centuries, a beautiful stub, before cranes returned in the nineteenth century to complete the original plan. When someone asked Antoni Gaudí why the Sagrada Família was taking so long, he is said to have replied, "My client is not in a hurry." The client, in his theology, was God; in ours, it would be the future. Either way, the building is a letter addressed to unborn strangers, and the address is written in patience.

Some letters to the future are alive. In the White Mountains of California grows a bristlecone pine known as Methuselah, which germinated around 2830 BCE — before the Great Pyramid rose, before Stonehenge's great stones were raised — and is still photosynthesizing today. It has watched the entire span of what we call history from a dry ridge at eleven thousand feet. The species holds a darker record too: in 1964, a graduate student coring trees on Wheeler Peak in Nevada got his bore tool stuck in a bristlecone nicknamed Prometheus, and the Forest Service permitted felling the tree to retrieve it. The ring count came back at nearly five thousand years. Researchers had accidentally cut down the oldest known living thing on earth, and the discipline has carried the embarrassment ever since — a small parable about how casually the present treats the past's property. Elsewhere, the boundaries get stranger: the aspen clone called Pando in Utah may be a single organism, one root system bearing forty-seven thousand trunks, that has persisted for thousands of years, possibly tens of thousands. Churchyards in Britain hold yews older than the churches built beside them. We are mayflies gardening redwoods.

⁂

Then there is the problem we created on purpose, which makes cathedral-builders look like optimists. Plutonium-239, a component of nuclear waste, has a half-life of 24,100 years, and the waste we have already produced will remain genuinely dangerous for something on the order of 100,000 years. Writing has existed for about 5,000. Every institution you have ever heard of is younger than 1,500. The task, stated plainly, is to send a message twenty times farther into the future than the entire span of literacy — to warn beings we cannot imagine about dangers they did not create, in languages that will not exist, using concepts that may not survive translation.

In the 1980s, the United States began confronting this seriously. The planned Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in New Mexico prompted a Human Interference Task Force, and Sandia National Laboratories convened a marker-design team that included, remarkably, archaeologists, linguists, astronomers, and materials scientists — people accustomed to asking how cultures remember and how things endure. Their proposal was architectural as much as textual: massive earthen berms arranged in threatening shapes, magnets buried in the soil so the site could be found by anyone sweeping with instruments, radar reflectors, granite monoliths carved with agonized faces, and messages rendered in seven languages, among them Navajo.

It is the message that has outlived the engineering. Drafted to be intelligible to a reader with no shared context, it abandons technical vocabulary entirely and speaks in the cadence of scripture or curse:

> *This place is a message… and part of a system of messages… pay attention to it! Sending this message was important to us. We considered ourselves to be a powerful culture.*
>
> *This place is not a place of honor… no highly esteemed deed is commemorated here… nothing valued is here.*
>
> *What is here was dangerous and repulsive to us. This message is a warning about danger.*
>
> *The danger is still present, in your time, as it was in ours.*
>
> *The danger is to the body, and it can kill.*

Read it aloud and notice what your nervous system does. The passage circulates online now as a meme, sampled in video games and creepypastas, because it sounds exactly like the warning scrawled above a sealed door in a horror story. That reception misses the point only superficially. The authors wanted visceral unease in a reader ten thousand years distant, and they got it immediately in readers ten thousand days distant. The message works because it does not argue; it haunts.

Other proposals went further into strangeness. The semiotician Thomas Sebeok, studying the problem in 1984, concluded that no engineered sign could be trusted to survive, but that folklore reliably does — and so he suggested creating an "atomic priesthood": a ritual institution that would transmit the truth of the site's danger disguised as religious taboo, renewed and reinterpreted by each generation, because dogma outlives blueprints. Around the same time, two European scholars proposed breeding "ray cats" — cats genetically altered to change color in the presence of radiation — and seeding songs and proverbs about them into the culture, so that biology and legend would propagate together: *if the cat turns green, flee the scene.* Decades later, musicians actually held a contest and wrote those songs. It sounds absurd until you notice that the Vedas were transmitted orally for three thousand years with astonishing fidelity, while no steel structure of comparable age remains standing anywhere on earth.

At Onkalo, on an island in Finland, engineers are finishing the world's first permanent deep geological repository, entombing waste in copper canisters four hundred meters down in bedrock. The documentary *Into Eternity* records the planners wrestling with the same questions and arriving at a possibility the opposite of the American instinct: perhaps the safest course is to bury the site and then erase every trace of its existence — no markers, no memory, nothing to attract the curious. Sometimes the deepest message is silence. Our ancestors may have intuited this first: some archaeologists suspect that Göbekli Tepe, the twelve-thousand-year-old temple complex in Turkey, was deliberately and carefully backfilled by its own builders, entombed by the people who loved it most.

⁂

Not everything we throw at the future is a warning. In 1977 the Voyager probes carried golden records: ninety minutes of music from Bach to Chuck Berry, greetings in fifty-five languages, whale song, and — in one of the tenderest gestures in the history of instrumentation — the recorded brainwaves of Ann Druyan, captured as she sat and thought about falling in love with the project's creative director, whom she would soon marry. The record is a bottle in the ocean of interstellar space; in about forty thousand years, Voyager 1 will drift past the star Gliese 445, closer to another sun than to ours, still playing.

The Long Now Foundation, founded in 1996, approached the problem from the direction of hope rather than hazard. Brian Eno coined the group's name after noticing that New York City, a place of millions, had compressed everyone's horizon to "here and now." Danny Hillis, the computer architect who dreamed up the project's centerpiece, liked to observe that when he was a child people talked about the year 2000, and that ever since, the future had been shrinking by one year per year for his entire life. His remedy is a clock — being assembled inside a limestone mountain in West Texas, on land owned by Jeff Bezos — designed to run unattended for ten thousand years, powered by day-night temperature differentials, ticking once a year, advancing its century hand once per century, releasing a cuckoo once per millennium, chiming melodies generated by an algorithm of Eno's devising that will not repeat within the clock's lifespan. Nobody will watch it. That is the point. The clock is less a machine than a myth with gears, an object whose mere existence is meant to stretch the imagination the way a cathedral stretches the neck.

Other experiments dot the landscape. Jem Finer's *Longplayer*, a musical composition for singing bowls, began playing on January 1, 2000, and is scored to continue, without repetition, for a thousand years. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores backup copies of the world's crops in permafrost — though after unusually warm weather in 2017, meltwater intruded partway into its entrance tunnel, a reminder that even our archives have a climate problem. The Georgia Guidestones, an anonymous granite monument erected in 1980 with instructions for humanity inscribed in eight languages, was bombed in 2022 and demolished the same day. It lasted forty-two years. The future, apparently, sometimes arrives early and brings explosives.

⁂

All of this runs up against a hard limit: language itself decays faster than stone. A modern English speaker cannot parse *Beowulf*, separated from us by a millennium; Chaucer requires translation; Shakespeare requires footnotes. If a thousand years does this to a language spoken continuously by hundreds of millions, what hope has a warning of surviving ten thousand? And yet the oral traditions whisper a subversive answer: the Vedas survived three millennia of transmission by mouth with remarkable accuracy, preserved not by institutions but by meter, repetition, and reverence. Stories, it turns out, are more durable than steel. Which is why the most sober analysts of nuclear semiotics keep circling back to the same uncomfortable conclusion: if you want to reach the deep future, you must stop writing manuals and start founding myths.

Lift your eyes and the scale tips over entirely. The light arriving tonight from the Andromeda galaxy left home two and a half million years ago, before our genus existed; the night sky is an archive of dead presents. In five billion years the sun will swell and cook the inner planets. Star formation will gutter out in a hundred trillion years; the last black holes will evaporate on the order of 10¹⁰⁰ years. These are numbers after which meaning stops being a relevant category. And yet the response of the clockmakers seems exactly right: build the clock to tick once a year, so slowly that no human schedule can synchronize with it, because the goal was never timekeeping. The goal is recalibration. Deep time offers a double gift, and both halves matter: it diminishes us honestly, and it obligates us completely. We are temporary, and therefore we are responsible — the only generation, ever, positioned exactly here.

Which returns everything to the present tense. Somewhere in the White Mountains, Methuselah is adding a ring this spring, indifferent to the fall of Rome and the invention of the semiconductor alike. Somewhere in the far future — year 12,000, say — a reader stands before a berm in the New Mexican desert, translating our warning syllable by syllable, and to that reader *we* are the ancients. Our "powerful culture" is their legend. The message is our epitaph and our gift, both at once. The abyss of time looks back at us only if we leave it something to say. The pine, for its part, is saying it already, one slow ring at a time, in the only tense that has ever existed.
